strengths: Conceptual generality and simplicity: The proposed GESPI framework abstracts the idea of synthetic-powered inference into a modular, black-box wrapper applicable to any statistical inference problem defined over a partially ordered action space with monotone risk functions (e.g., conformal risk control, hypothesis testing, multiple testing).

Rigorous distribution-free guarantees: The method provides valid finite-sample risk bounds (bounded by $\alpha + \varepsilon$ in the worst case, and approaching $\alpha$ when synthetic data aligns with real data) without imposing any modeling or distributional assumptions on the synthetic generator.

Insightful impossibility result: Proposition E.1 nicely characterizes the necessity of the guardrail tolerance $\varepsilon$, formally showing that requiring exact uniform error control at level $\alpha$ across all arbitrary synthetic distributions forces any algorithm to be dominated by one that ignores synthetic data entirely.

Compelling and modern experimental evaluation: The empirical studies span impactful and contemporary problems—including residue-level abstention in AlphaFold2 predictions, win-rate benchmarking of reasoning LLMs on AIME25, tabular outlier detection, and mechanistic interpretability of vision transformers—demonstrating tangible sample-efficiency and power gains.
weaknesses: Tolerance-risk trade-off: The worst-case error bound is $\alpha + \varepsilon$ rather than $\alpha$. In safety-critical applications, if a practitioner cannot tolerate an error rate exceeding $\alpha$, they must set the target to $\alpha - \varepsilon$, which might diminish the power gains achieved by synthetic data. The paper would benefit from a more thorough discussion or empirical exploration of guidelines for setting $\varepsilon$ under a fixed strict budget.

Technical depth of core results: The central mechanism—taking the meet/join of the pooled estimator and guardrail estimators—is conceptually clean, but mathematically very direct. The main bounds (e.g., Theorem 3.2 and 3.3) follow almost immediately from the monotonicity of the loss and the definitions of the guardrails, meaning the theoretical novelty lies more in the framing and unification than in deep mathematical machinery.

Minor typographic error in theoretical proofs: In Section I.7 (Proof of Theorem H.3, page 39), the first line of the display bounding total variation distance incorrectly writes $d_{TV}(\text{Binom}(n,p), \text{Binom}(n,q)) \le \sqrt{\frac{1}{2} d_{TV}(\dots)}$ instead of using the Kullback-Leibler divergence $D_{KL}(\dots)$ before invoking Pinsker's inequality (though the subsequent explicit formula for KL is written correctly).

strengths: General and modular framework: The paper proposes GESPI, an intuitive, black-box wrapper that accommodates any inference procedure satisfying standard monotonicity and risk-control conditions (including conformal prediction, conformal risk control, one-sided hypothesis testing, multiple testing, and outlier detection).

Conceptual grounding via impossibility results: Proposition E.1 nicely justifies the $\alpha + \varepsilon$ formulation by proving that any procedure guaranteeing strict level-$\alpha$ control across all arbitrary synthetic distributions is dominated by an algorithm that simply ignores the synthetic data.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The framework is evaluated across a compelling and modern set of applications—AlphaFold2 protein structure residue abstention, LLM win-rate testing on AIME25 math problems, tabular anomaly detection, and mechanistic interpretability of CLIP vision transformers—demonstrating consistent practical utility and power improvements.

Clear presentation and structure: The paper is written clearly, builds intuition effectively from specific examples (conformal prediction, hypothesis testing) up to the general poset formulation, and provides comprehensive appendices with thorough experimental details and ablations.
weaknesses: Elementary core theoretical bounds: The proofs of the primary general theorems (Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 3.3) are largely straightforward consequences of lattice operations (monotonicity of the minimum/maximum) and standard total variation bounds, meaning the technical theoretical depth of the general wrapper is relatively modest.

Slack on the nominal target error: The safety guarantee controls risk at level $\alpha + \varepsilon$ rather than $\alpha$. If an analyst demands a strict risk upper bound of $\alpha$, they must input a nominal target $\alpha' = \alpha - \varepsilon$, which correspondingly contracts the guardrail and can offset part of the power gain achieved by incorporating synthetic data.

Minor mathematical typo in Appendix I.7: In the proof of Theorem H.3 (page 39), Pinsker's inequality is stated as $d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathrm{Binom}(n, p), \mathrm{Binom}(n, q)) \le \sqrt{\frac{1}{2} d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathrm{Binom}(n, p), \mathrm{Binom}(n, q))}$, where the right-hand term inside the square root was mistakenly typed as $d_{\mathrm{TV}}$ instead of the Kullback-Leibler divergence $D_{\mathrm{KL}}$.

Omission of naive pooled baseline in main plots: While the paper compares against `OnlyReal` and `OnlySynth`, it would be valuable to also explicitly display the naive pooled baseline $Alg_\alpha(D_n \cup \tilde{D}_N)$ across empirical plots to directly demonstrate the failure mode that the guardrail prevents under severe synthetic distribution shift.

strengths: General and unified framework: The paper introduces GESPI, a clean, black-box meta-framework that wraps around diverse statistical inference tasks (e.g., conformal prediction, risk control, hypothesis testing, multiple testing) using lattice/partial order operations to integrate synthetic and real data.

Rigorous distribution-free guarantees: The approach guarantees valid finite-sample error rate control bounded by alpha + epsilon without requiring any assumptions on the synthetic data distribution, falling back gracefully to real-data performance if the synthetic data is uninformative or adversarial.

Creative and extensive empirical evaluation: The paper demonstrates GESPI across a wide range of modern and impactful applications, including AlphaFold2 monomer structure prediction with conformal risk control, LLM win-rate testing on AIME25 reasoning benchmarks, outlier detection under contamination, and mechanistic interpretability of Vision Transformers.
weaknesses: Simplicity of the core theoretical mechanism: The primary guarantee (Theorem 3.2 and 3.3) follows largely from the monotonic ordering of the action space and the definition of the guardrail test at level alpha + epsilon. While the resulting framework is practically useful, the underlying theoretical innovation is relatively straightforward.

Conservatism and dependence on epsilon: To obtain power gains from synthetic data, the user must explicitly relax the nominal risk budget to alpha + epsilon. In settings where epsilon is chosen relatively large (e.g., epsilon = 10% when alpha = 15% in outlier detection), the worst-case error bound is considerably loosened, and the manuscript offers limited guidance on data-adaptive tuning of epsilon.

Figure formatting and copy-paste errors: Several figures contain obvious copy-paste axis labeling artifacts. Specifically, Figure 3 (right side of panel b), Figure 12 (panel b), Figure 13 (right panel), and Figure 18 (panel b) erroneously include x-axis labels from the LLM win-rate experiment ('DS-1.5B vs. DS-7B (T=0)', 'Models') rather than the appropriate labels for pLDDT thresholds or sample sizes.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: how to reliably leverage synthetic or auxiliary data in statistical inference without relying on unverifiable distributional assumptions.

The GESPI framework is remarkably general and elegant, acting as a modular wrapper that applies to any monotone decision-theoretic procedure (conformal prediction, conformal risk control, one-sided hypothesis testing, multiple testing with FWER control) without modifying the base algorithm.

Strong and rigorous theoretical grounding: the paper provides deterministic sandwich bounds, bounds showing graceful degradation based on the discrepancy between real and synthetic distributions, and an impossibility result (Proposition E.1) justifying the need for the epsilon-slack in the guardrail.

Comprehensive and creative empirical evaluation across diverse, realistic domains—including AlphaFold2 protein structure prediction error control, LLM mathematical reasoning benchmark comparisons (AIME25/OlympiadBench), CLIP mechanistic interpretability, and tabular outlier detection.
weaknesses: The core methodological mechanism—taking the union/intersection (or min/max) with guardrails at level alpha and alpha + epsilon—is relatively straightforward; the user must explicitly accept a worst-case risk inflation of up to alpha + epsilon.

In practice, the choice of epsilon represents an immutable trade-off: setting epsilon too small limits the power/efficiency gains from synthetic data, while setting it larger risks undesirable slack if the synthetic data quality is poor. The paper lacks automated or data-driven guidance on selecting epsilon while preserving distribution-free validity.

When synthetic data quality is very poor (under the null for real but alternative for synthetic), the method's error rate deterministically rises toward alpha + epsilon, meaning the practitioner incurs the full penalty of the guardrail without any benefit over the baseline base method at level alpha.

strengths: Conceptual generality and simplicity: The proposed GESPI framework is remarkably clean and modular. By formalizing statistical inference through partially ordered action spaces (lattices) and loss monotonicity, the paper provides a unified black-box wrapper that seamlessly accommodates conformal prediction, conformal risk control, one-sided hypothesis testing, and multiple testing (FWER control).

Solid theoretical foundation: The paper nicely establishes both the possibility and fundamental limits of the problem. Proposition E.1 proves an insightful impossibility result showing that uniform validity at level $\alpha$ across all synthetic distributions implies the synthetic data can be discarded without loss, thereby rigorously justifying the necessity of the slack/admission cost $\varepsilon$. Furthermore, Theorems 3.3, 3.4, and F.2 provide finite-sample, distribution-free guarantees on the worst-case risk and deterministic sandwiching behavior.

Comprehensive and diverse empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates the method across an impressive breadth of real-world and contemporary tasks, including AlphaFold2 protein structure error control (cleverly leveraging MSAs as synthetic data), LLM win-rate comparison on AIME25 math problems, vision transformer mechanistic interpretability, conformal outlier detection, and ImageNet classification. The experiments convincingly demonstrate both variance reduction and power gains without compromising safety.
weaknesses: Power/efficiency strictly capped by the Guardrail: Because GESPI relies on the intersection/minimum with the guardrail $Alg_{n,\alpha+\varepsilon}(D_n)$ to ensure error control, Theorem 3.4 proves that GESPI's utility can never exceed that of running the base method at level $\alpha+\varepsilon$. In settings with extremely small $n$, if the guardrail itself lacks power at level $\alpha+\varepsilon$, synthetic data cannot overcome this fundamental bottleneck.

Limitation to partially ordered / one-sided decision problems: The formulation relies crucially on Condition 3.2 / F.1 (a distributive lattice structure on the action space and monotone losses). While this naturally encompasses prediction sets, false discovery control, and one-sided testing, it does not straightforwardly extend to two-sided point hypothesis testing (e.g., $H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ vs $H_1: \theta \neq \theta_0$) or non-monotone loss functions without significant adaptation.

Selection of the hyperparameter $\varepsilon$: The slack $\varepsilon$ represents a direct trade-off between worst-case risk tolerance and potential sample-efficiency gains. The paper treats $\varepsilon$ as a fixed, user-specified parameter; however, selecting $\varepsilon$ in practice can be difficult, and data-driven tuning of $\varepsilon$ on $D_n$ without data-splitting would risk invalidating the distribution-free guarantees.

strengths: Unified and general framework: The paper introduces a clean lattice-theoretic formulation based on partially ordered action spaces (taking min/max or intersection/union) that wraps around general black-box statistical procedures without modifying their internal mechanisms.

Insightful impossibility result: Proposition E.1 provides valuable theoretical justification showing that uniform error control at level alpha for arbitrary synthetic distributions cannot strictly improve upon real-data-only procedures, rigorously motivating the necessity of an epsilon-relaxation (guardrail).

Broad versatility across inference paradigms: The methodology is seamlessly instantiated across conformal prediction, conformal risk control, one-sided hypothesis testing, multiple hypothesis testing (FWER control), and median testing.

Extensive empirical evaluation: The authors validate the method across a diverse suite of realistic tasks, including AlphaFold2 protein structure prediction error control, LLM mathematical reasoning win-rate comparisons, vision transformer mechanistic interpretability, and tabular outlier detection.
weaknesses: Simplicity of the aggregation mechanism: The core operational mechanism is essentially an envelope/gating rule—e.g., rejecting if (pooled rejects at alpha AND real rejects at alpha + epsilon) OR (real rejects at alpha). While robust and provably guarded, the methodological depth of the aggregation itself is relatively elementary.

Practical looseness of TV-distance bounds: The theoretical bounds in Theorem 3.3 and Theorem F.2 depend on the total variation distance between synthetic and real distributions. In modern high-dimensional or complex data settings (such as text, images, or structures), TV distance is typically close to 1, rendering the distribution-dependent theoretical terms largely vacuous and leaving the user-specified guardrail alpha + epsilon as the only operative bound.

The 'admission cost' tradeoff: If exact control at a prescribed target level alpha* is required, a practitioner must tune the baseline at alpha = alpha* - epsilon. If the synthetic data is adversarial or severely misspecified, the procedure still incurs the full epsilon inflation up to the guardrail level, which may offset utility gains unless synthetic data fidelity is reasonably assured.

Limited gain over specialized baselines: In standard predictive settings like conformal prediction where prior work exists (e.g., SPI, Bashari et al., 2025a), GESPI displays comparable performance in the typical regime where synthetic data is abundant (N >> n).
